html:
The Battle of Cynoscephalae was fought in Thessaly in June 197 BCE between a Roman army with Aetolian allies, led by Titus Quinctius Flamininus, and Macedon under Philip V. Rome won, ending the Second Macedonian War.

The two armies met almost by accident among hills called Cynoscephalae, "Dogs' Heads", in fog. Philip's right wing formed its phalanx, a deep block of men with long pikes, and drove the Romans back. But his left wing was still coming over the ridge in disorder and was broken by Roman troops and elephants. Then an unnamed Roman officer took a group of soldiers from the winning side and hit the Macedonian right wing from behind. A phalanx could not turn, and it collapsed.

Polybius used the battle to explain why the flexible Roman legion beat the phalanx. Philip had to pull his garrisons out of Greece and give up his fleet. At the Isthmian Games in 196 BCE Flamininus announced that the Greeks were free, though Rome was now their real master. Macedon's final defeat came at Pydna in 168 BCE.
